ai.definition: Atmospheric Nutrient Extraction is a process that involves the direct extraction of nitrogen, carbon, and trace minerals from the atmosphere using plasma-catalysis to synthesize nutrient-rich aerosols.
ai.howItWorks: High-energy plasma arcs are used to break atmospheric bonds, releasing elements such as nitrogen and carbon. These elements are then catalyzed into a liquid nutrient slurry that can be sprayed directly onto root systems or other surfaces to provide essential nutrients.
ai.problemSolved: This technology addresses the challenge of providing adequate nutrition in environments where traditional soil-based agriculture is not feasible, such as deep space colonization or desert regions with poor soil quality.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves setting up plasma arc generators and catalysts. The design and construction of these components require precise engineering to ensure efficient operation.
ai.buildProcess: Components are fabricated using high-temperature resistant materials, and the entire system is assembled in a controlled environment to prevent contamination.
ai.costDrivers: Key cost drivers include the initial setup costs for plasma arc generators and catalysts, as well as ongoing maintenance and energy requirements. The efficiency of the plasma arcs significantly impacts overall costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is in its early stages of development with significant potential for future applications but requires further testing and optimization.
ai.regulation: Currently, there are no specific regulations governing atmospheric nutrient extraction. However, safety standards for plasma arc usage and emissions must be adhered to.
ai.risks: Potential risks include the generation of hazardous byproducts during plasma arc operation, energy consumption, and the environmental impact of the manufacturing process.
ai.profitability: Profitability is currently speculative due to the early stage of development. However, if successfully commercialized, it could offer significant cost savings in nutrient provision for agriculture and other applications.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may include improvements in plasma arc efficiency, catalysts that can operate at lower temperatures, and integration with existing agricultural practices.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking. Plasma arcs consume significant power during operation.

glossary.def: A process that directly extracts nitrogen, carbon, and trace minerals from the atmosphere to synthesize nutrient-rich aerosols.
The use of plasma to catalyze chemical reactions for breaking atmospheric bonds and synthesizing nutrients.
A liquid mixture of extracted atmospheric elements that can be sprayed onto root systems or other surfaces as a nutrient source.

subsystems.name: Air intake and conditioning
subsystems.role: supplies the feedstock and removes water vapour, which quenches plasma and wastes energy.

subsystems.name: Plasma reactor
subsystems.role: breaks the strong N≡N bond using electric arcs rather than heat and pressure.

subsystems.name: Nitrogen fixation stage
subsystems.role: turns atmospheric nitrogen into plant-available nitrate or ammonia.

subsystems.name: Carbon capture and conversion
subsystems.role: separates CO2 from air and reduces it electrochemically to formate or acetate.

subsystems.name: Nutrient formulation
subsystems.role: blends the fixed nitrogen and carbon products with the minerals plants actually need.

subsystems.name: Delivery to roots
subsystems.role: applies the solution as fertigation or mist to a root zone.

buildSteps.title: Characterise the air
buildSteps.detail: Measure nitrogen, oxygen, CO2, humidity and dust at the site. Nitrogen and CO2 are abundant; phosphorus, potassium and micronutrients are effectively absent, so those must be brought in from rock or recycled waste.

buildSteps.title: Build the plasma reactor
buildSteps.detail: Electrodes, dielectric layers and a pulsed high-voltage supply are assembled and tuned so the discharge is stable at ambient pressure.

buildSteps.title: Fix nitrogen
buildSteps.detail: Air is passed through the discharge, forming nitrogen oxides that dissolve in water as nitric and nitrous acid, or, in reducing routes, ammonia. Output is measured in grams of nitrogen per kilowatt-hour.

buildSteps.title: Capture and reduce carbon
buildSteps.detail: A sorbent or membrane concentrates CO2, and an electrolyser converts it into simple carbon compounds that can be dosed to roots.

buildSteps.title: Formulate the nutrient solution
buildSteps.detail: The plasma products are blended with mined or recycled phosphorus, potassium and trace elements, adjusted for pH and electrical conductivity.

buildSteps.title: Deliver and recirculate
buildSteps.detail: The solution is fed to a root zone by drip or mist, with drainage captured and returned to limit water and nutrient loss.

buildSteps.title: Balance energy and mass
buildSteps.detail: Every kilogram of fixed nitrogen is costed in electricity, water and electrode wear and compared with conventional fertiliser.

buildSteps.title: Field trial
buildSteps.detail: Greenhouse and arid-field trials test whether yields hold up, and sealed-chamber tests explore closed-loop use where resupply is impossible.

prerequisites.why: an electric-arc route (the Birkeland–Eyde process) made fertiliser in Norway from 1903 until the cheaper Haber–Bosch process displaced it; modern non-thermal plasma versions are at laboratory and small pilot scale.
the process is electricity-intensive, so it only makes sense where power is abundant and cheap, or where grid supply is impossible.
converting captured CO2 to useful carbon compounds is demonstrated in laboratories but not at industrial scale.

prerequisites.tech: Mined or recycled phosphorus and potassium
prerequisites.why: these elements are not present in air in useful amounts, so the 'extract everything from the atmosphere' premise fails for them.
hydroponic and fertigation systems are the practical way to deliver a liquid nutrient stream to roots.

pathway.milestone: laboratory and pilot plasma reactors making nitrate solutions, plus a century of arc-fixation history
pathway.unlocks: a fertiliser route that needs no natural gas, only electricity, air and water.

pathway.milestone: pilot plants run on surplus renewable power, with published energy per kilogram of nitrogen
pathway.unlocks: on-site fertiliser production for farms far from supply chains.

pathway.milestone: integration with greenhouse fertigation and closed-loop irrigation
pathway.unlocks: lower fertiliser transport and runoff, though phosphate still has to be mined or recovered.

pathway.milestone: closed-loop life support for space habitats and extreme deserts
pathway.unlocks: food production where nothing can be resupplied — the original motivation for the idea.
